newsitem.title: USA: US chip industry Dec book-to-bill seen about 1.15.
newsitem.headline: US chip industry Dec book-to-bill seen about 1.15.

text.p: The U.S. chip industry's barometer of health, the book-to-bill ratio, is expected to show orders towered above sales again in December.

Analysts said they expect a December ratio of 1.14 to 1.15 to be reported by the industry's trade grouop later this week. That would be even with 1.15 in November -- the highest ratio in more than a year. A 1.15 ratio means orders were worth 115 percent of sales booked.
"Another good number" analyst Rob Chaplinsky of Hambrecht & Quist predicted for December, estimating 1.14 to 1.16.
"It'll be driven by Intel seeing very strong bookings in its CPU business," and "more stable pricing" in the industry, Chaplinsky said.
Memory chip makers like Micron Technology Inc and Texas Instruments Inc saw memory prices slide steeply during most of 1996.
Bear Stearns analyst Nimal Vallipuram cited 1.14 or "marginally lower than November," the peak order month for holiday season sales for chips going into personal computers.
UBS Securities' Charles Boucher cited flat with November.
December's report will be the last the U.S. Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA) releases on American chip makers. The gruop will replace it with a report on global sales of semiconductor chips.

Many U.S. chip makers make 50 to 60 percent of their sales on overseas markets. Criticism of the SIA's book to bill report has mounted in the past two years, with the numbers seen as limited and not representative of the whole industry.
The SIA agreed the Americas-only report was becoming less useful with the increasingly global nature of the semiconductor industry, so it decided to make the changes.
But the new global report will not discuss bookings, which analysts said were the most useful information in the report -- a forward indicator of future sales and industry health.
The stock market has traditionally watched the book-to- bill report closely, and chip stocks often undergo wild swings shortly after the report.
Some analysts said the absence of the Americas booking report could increase the volatility.
"It will be interesting to see if it will increase volatility or decrease it," Boucher said of no report.
"I think it will increase it because there will be more speculation and less certainty," he said, adding that the more information the market has, the better.

Yet several others, such as Vallipuram, said they think some other report will soon evolve to take the place of the trade association's report, such as an independent research firm's industry-wide estimate.
"The information was not fully accurate," he said of the SIA's book to bill report. "But the vacuum could create uncertainty in the market."
